It is not a thing or substance with essential attributes that are inalienable, eternal, unchanging, and dependent only on itself.
We will see later what that something is.

But even now we can say this much: the human I cannot exist apart from a natural body existing within the world, and the existence of the I consists entirely in interaction with that world—an interaction that changes both the I and the world.
Understood in this way, the I not only fails to imply or require the existence of God. It actually excludes it.
If such an I exists, then God does not.
And if God existed, such an I would be impossible.
In one sense, this makes philosophy’s task easier.
We do not need to know God in order to know ourselves.
In other words, to answer questions about ourselves, we do not have to answer questions about God—unless we count the statement “God does not exist” as an answer to one of them.
But this simplification is more than offset by another requirement.
Once we speak about humanity, we must also speak about the world and about history.
If a person’s qualities are shaped through interaction with the world, then to know what a human being is we must also know the natural world as a whole.
And because every concrete human being is also an historical being, that person is shaped by a particular place in history and by interaction with the social and political world in which he lives.
So to know humanity, we must also know this historical world in its entirety.
Since there is no divine world and everything that exists belongs to nature and history, we have to say that a human being can be fully known only when we know absolutely everything.

True and concrete self-consciousness, or fully achieved self-awareness, is therefore nothing other than perfect knowledge in general: knowledge of everything that exists and, all the more, everything that can be known.
The philosopher reaches his goal—becomes able to answer every question about his life and activity—only when he becomes omniscient.
In other words, “wisdom” is identical with perfect knowledge.
And that is precisely the kind of knowledge theologians traditionally attribute to God.
So it is hardly surprising, as I have already said, that most philosophers regarded wisdom as inaccessible to human beings.
What should surprise us is that some thinkers had the extraordinary audacity to look for it not in God but in themselves, while knowing—as Hegel did—that “wisdom” nevertheless means omniscience.

To know this and still remain a philosopher is consciously to seek the kind of knowledge that human beings had previously dared to attribute only to God: perfect, or “absolute,” knowledge—omniscience.
Strange or not, philosophers of this kind have existed, and still do.
So too is anyone who genuinely deserves to call himself a Marxist and, for that reason, an authentic Hegelian.

In the next chapter, then, we will have to examine philosophy understood in this Marxist-Hegelian sense: the striving for “wisdom,” which is to say the striving for complete self-awareness, or fully achieved self-consciousness understood as perfect knowledge or omniscience.
But we must begin with this “wisdom” understood as perfect knowledge.
The idea of the philosophical system

We have seen that complete, concrete self-awareness in fact amounts to omniscience. It means answering exhaustively every question about oneself, and therefore also answering every question about everything that concretely and really exists.

We will now show not only that complete self-awareness—that is, full and concrete self-awareness—amounts to omniscience, to “perfect” or “absolute” knowledge, but also that such knowledge is itself full and concrete awareness in the absolute sense. In other words, to know everything about any concrete phenomenon, being, or thing is to know everything that can be known at all. To say everything that can be said about something that concretely exists is, in the end, to say everything that can be said in any way whatever.

Everything that exists really exists concretely. And everything real occupies a determinate position or place in a space and time that are not “empty,” but are filled with material phenomena and processes immediately and inseparably connected with one another. Conversely, everything that exists in this way is “real and concrete.” Everything real is concrete, and everything concrete is real. And everything real or concrete is either material or immediately and inseparably connected with something material.

Every material thing exists both in space and in time. This means that it occupies a determinate position in space and time. We all more or less “understand” what these words mean when we use them, although we are far from always knowing exactly what they involve. So there is no need to stop here and define them. It is enough for us to “understand” what it means to “occupy a position in space and time”—to understand statements such as “to be at a certain point in space” and “to exist, or to come into being and pass away, within a certain interval of time.”
Once we understand this, we also understand that in “empty” space-time every point and every moment would be identical. We could not distinguish one from another without appealing to something else.

We call this “something else” matter. Although matter is connected with space and time, it must also be distinct from them. Matter is what allows us, first, to locate something in space and time and, second, to distinguish the place and moment it occupies from all the rest of space and time.

In other words, matter is a spatio-temporal “something” that introduces differences into space and time and thereby makes it possible to measure them. Matter itself is then measured by units of space and time—say, centimetres and seconds—and also by a unit peculiar to matter itself, such as grams. What is measured by this last kind of unit, the specifically material unit, we call mass.
We can therefore say that matter is mass extended through space and enduring through time. By being measurable itself, it also lets us measure the space and time that it occupies.

But if we are pressed to say what this “something” actually is—what “matter” is in itself—the question becomes extremely difficult, perhaps impossible, to answer. The physical nature of matter is revealed through mathematical formulas rather than through ordinary logical discourse.
It is possible, however, to define matter in relation to human beings, and a number of philosophers have done this correctly. The definition can be reduced to the following.

Matter is the “something” in space and time that is, in some sense, impenetrable to me: something I can run into or touch, something that resists my action, something that can injure me and, ultimately, kill me.
And all this happens immediately—that is, without the mediation of another human being.
In other words, the “material” or natural world is simply the concrete, real world in which I could ultimately be killed—that is, cease to be conscious—even if I were the only human being in it.
Let me make this clearer with a few examples.

The famous roof tile falling on my head, or a lightning bolt falling from the sky, can kill me whether or not I am the last human being on Earth. Their effect on me is immediate. That is why they are real, concrete, and material.
The Christian God is quite different.

God is plainly immaterial, if only because he has no real existence at all. Yet God can act on me and can even kill me. If, for example, I had lived in the Middle Ages and spread false information about him—“heresies”—he might have killed me by having me burned at the stake.

But he could not have done this immediately. To execute me, he would have needed other human beings to carry out his orders. It would have been these people—or, more precisely, their bodies—that directly killed me, acting as intermediaries between God’s will and my death.

Take another example, closer to our own time. A court sentences me to death. In one sense, it is a word that kills me: the sentence that is written down and read aloud. Without that word, I might have gone on living quite peacefully.

Yet the sentence cannot kill me immediately. Another human being is still required as an intermediary. That person kills me with his body, acting on the basis of the order contained in the sentence. Without this mediation, the sentence could exist and I could still go on living.
So the “word”—the legal sentence—exists and acts indirectly. It is the first cause of my death. But it is not material.

If we call anything that has effects—that is, anything whose existence changes the existence of something else—“effective” or “existent,” then both the sentence and the body carrying it out must count as forms of existence. But because the sentence acts on me indirectly, while the body acts on me directly, only the body is material and real.
We can therefore divide everything that exists or has effects into two fundamentally different kinds.

The first kind can act on me immediately—ultimately, it can kill me or deprive me of consciousness without needing another person as an intermediary. This kind of existence is material, real, and concrete. It extends through space, endures through time, and can be measured in units of space, time, and “mass.”

The second kind can act on me—can ultimately kill me—only through another human being. This kind of existence is non-material, non-real, and non-concrete. Nor can it be measured in units of space and time, because it has no spatial extension and does not endure in time in the same way.

This second kind of existence is usually called ideal existence, from the Greek word idea, which Plato made famous in philosophy and which corresponds to what in Russian is called a general “concept.”

The world of immediate action is the world of things—the genuinely concrete, real, material world. The world of action mediated through human beings, by contrast, is the world of ideal, abstract, non-material “things.” Above all, it is the world of general concepts—in other words, of meaningful words.
A simple example will make this clearer.

Take a particular table: a concrete, real, material table. It has a definite size, shape, colour, and so on. It stands in a particular place and was made at a particular time. It will exist for a certain period, and at some definite moment it will disappear in one way or another—that is, it will cease to be a table. I can also run into it and, conceivably, even die as a result.

It is completely impossible to assign this general “table” a particular shape, size, colour, and so on, since tables can be square, round, and many other things. The general concept of a table certainly includes the concept of space, but we cannot say where this “table in general” is located. Nor can we say when it came into existence.
It is, so to speak, everywhere and nowhere. While the material table grows old and eventually breaks, the general “table” remains unchanged.
It is plainly immaterial: we cannot say what material it is made of. And of course we cannot measure it in units of space, time, or mass. Nor can we bump into it and die.
Yet the “table in general” genuinely exists no less than any material table does.

This particular material table exists effectively when I can run into it; otherwise it may be nothing more than a mirage or optical illusion. The “table in general,” meanwhile, exists effectively when I understand what the word “table” means and when that meaning can make me act.
For example, it exists if, after hearing the order “buy a table,” I really do buy a table—one I can actually bump into—rather than buying something completely different.
This effectively existing “table in general” is what we call “ideal,” “abstract,” and “non-material.”

There can therefore be no doubt that everything that exists falls into two worlds: the world of real, concrete, material things, and the world of ideal, abstract, non-material “things,” which exist within the material world in the form of words that are spoken, written, or thought.
But this still does not exhaust everything that exists.

Alongside the world of ideal things and real things, with their definite and fixed qualities, there is also the human world. It consists of beings that should not properly be called “things” at all because, as we will see later, they have no fixed qualities.
A human being cannot be placed entirely within either of the two worlds just described.
A human being is not an ideal “thing,” because he is present in the material world in the form of what we call his body—a material thing—and not merely in the form of a word.

But neither is a human being a purely material thing, because ideal things can act on him immediately. If he hears the command “stand up,” for example, his body may rise without another human being having to intervene.

Human beings therefore belong to both worlds at once. They live and act as the link between them, serving as the intermediary through which one world can act on the other—an action that would otherwise be impossible.

I am walking somewhere and come up against a locked door that blocks my way. Everything here takes place within the real, material world. Even if I were sleepwalking—so that I lacked specifically human consciousness—I would still be stopped.
The door does not stop the human being as a human being. It stops the body. It would also stop an animal, a plant, or even, in another sense, light and wind.
If the door were open and I were asleep, I would simply pass through it, just as wind and light would.
Now suppose there is a sign above the doorway reading:
If this ideal “thing”—the prohibition on entering—“exists” for me, meaning that I understand the words whose material form strikes my senses, then I stop. Wind and light continue on their way.
My path is open in the material world but closed in the ideal world.
The fact that I stop in the material world, unlike animals and other non-human things, shows that I live and act not only in the material world but also in the ideal one.
The word itself does not act immediately on my body. If I am asleep, or if I do not understand the language, I will not stop.
Yet no mediation by another person is required. I mediate the action myself. I am my own intermediary between an ideal “thing”—the meaning of the words on the sign—and a real thing, namely my body.
A human being, then, is not merely a body and not merely a word. A human being is a body, a word, and the intermediary between the two.
This intermediary is the human I. It consists, on the one hand, in consciousness of the body and of words and, on the other, in self-awareness.
But this I is not itself the whole human being.
The human being is the body in which this I exists, and which the I uses to speak and to act according to the way it understands words.
